lesson.title: Fear and Accusation: The Rise of McCarthyism
lesson.summary: Amid the shocks of communist victory in China, a Soviet atomic bomb, and the Korean War, Senator Joseph McCarthy built a national following by making sweeping, often unsubstantiated accusations of communist infiltration, fueling a second Red Scare that ruined careers with little regard for evidence.
lesson.body:
The early Cold War produced a string of genuine shocks to American confidence: communist forces won China's civil war in 1949, the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb that same year, ending the American nuclear monopoly, and in 1950 American troops were fighting and dying in Korea against communist forces. Real cases of Soviet espionage also came to light, including the conviction of former State Department official Alger Hiss for perjury in 1950 and the 1951 conviction of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union, for which they were executed in 1953. Coming after the first Red Scare of 1919 and 1920, these events created fertile ground for a new wave of anti-communist anxiety, one that went well beyond reasonable concern into outright hysteria.

Into this atmosphere stepped Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin. In a speech in Wheeling, West Virginia, on February 9, 1950, McCarthy claimed to hold a list of communists working inside the State Department, though the number he cited shifted from one telling to the next and he never produced credible evidence to support the claim. What mattered politically was not the accuracy of McCarthy's charges but the fear and attention they generated. Historians who have examined the record closely have found that McCarthy's specific accusations were, in the overwhelming majority of cases, exaggerated, unsubstantiated, or simply false, but at the time few politicians dared publicly challenge him for fear of being branded soft on communism themselves.

McCarthy used his position, especially as chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations starting in 1953, to hold hearings that destroyed reputations and careers based on rumor, guilt by association, and refusal to answer questions, rather than proven wrongdoing. People lost their jobs, were blacklisted from their professions, or saw their lives upended simply for having attended a meeting years earlier or for refusing, on constitutional grounds, to answer questions about their political associations. This pattern, using accusation itself as a weapon regardless of evidence, and treating a person's silence or invocation of rights as proof of guilt, is what historians mean by the term McCarthyism: a style of reckless, unfounded accusation rather than any specific set of true findings.

McCarthy's downfall came during the Army-McCarthy hearings in the spring of 1954, when he turned his attention to the United States Army and the hearings were broadcast live on television, letting the American public watch his tactics directly for the first time. During the hearings, Army attorney Joseph Welch challenged McCarthy's treatment of a young lawyer on Welch's staff, a moment widely seen as turning public opinion decisively against the senator. The Senate formally censured McCarthy in December 1954, and his influence collapsed almost overnight. He died in 1957, but the climate of suspicion, and the willingness of investigators to treat accusation as equivalent to guilt, that he had helped create left lasting damage to civil liberties and due process in the United States.
